rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The debate over seeing God peaked from the early period through the Imams Jaʿfar and al-Riḍā; both disputing camps used this verse, and Ayyubid violence later destroyed the Muʿtazilites.
rows.anchor: كان النزاع والمشاجرة في الصدر الأول وخاصة في زمان الصادقين إلى زمان الرضا عليهم السلام في المسألة بالغا أوج شدته

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites deny vision absolutely, appealing to “You will not see Me” and rational and transmitted proofs against sight, while reinterpreting evidence that appears to permit it.
rows.anchor: ينكرها المعتزلة مطلقا ويثبتها الأشاعرة في الآخرة

rows.speaker: الأشاعرة
rows.claim: The Ashʿarites affirm vision in the afterlife, citing the verse’s mountain analogy and other verses and reports, while reinterpreting contrary evidence.
rows.anchor: يثبتها الأشاعرة في الآخرة وهناك طائفة أخرى تثبتها في الدنيا والآخرة جميعا

rows.speaker: طائفة أخرى
rows.claim: A third group affirms vision both in this world and the afterlife; both this group and the Ashʿarites use the verse as evidence.
rows.anchor: هناك طائفة أخرى تثبتها في الدنيا والآخرة جميعا

rows.speaker: الأشاعرة
rows.claim: They argue that nothing proves ocular perception must be restricted to bodies, so it could relate to immaterial things; because both substances and accidents are seen, they infer anything existent could be seen.
rows.anchor: لا دليل على وجوب انحصار الرؤية البصرية في الجسمانيات فمن الجائز أن يتعلق بغير الأمور المادية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says these two rational arguments and similar proofs have been shown false with near-self-evident clarity.
rows.anchor: وقد اتضح بطلان هاتين الحجتين وما يسانخهما من الحجج والأقاويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every form of ocular seeing is material and natural, involving measure, shape, color, light, and a physical faculty, so it cannot apply to God in this world or the afterlife; proofs and revelation deny it.
rows.anchor: هي معها مادية طبيعية متعلقة بقدر وشكل ولون وضوء تعملها أداة مادية طبيعية فإنها مستحيلة التعلق بالله سبحانه في الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Texts that affirm vision refer instead to a special, immediate necessary knowledge of God beyond knowledge gained by inference, whose setting is the afterlife.
rows.anchor: هناك علم ضروري خاص يتعلق به تعالى غير العلم الضروري الحاصل بالاستدلال تسمى رؤية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request “My Lord, show me” concerns heart vision as used in the reports, not ocular vision, whether as an affirmation, denial, request, or answer.
rows.anchor: أجنبية أصلا عن الرؤية البصرية الحسية إثباتا ونفيا وسؤالا وجوابا

rows.speaker: الرضا عليه السلام
rows.claim: In a report cited by al-Ṣadūq from al-Riḍā’s answer to al-Maʾmūn, Moses asked on behalf of his people: after their demand to see God openly and their revival, they insisted he ask for them.
rows.anchor: روى الصدوق في العيون فيما سأله المأمون عن الرضا عليه السلام أنه أجاب عن سؤال الرؤية في الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls that report weak in transmission and inconsistent with established principles in the Imams’ reports, which repeatedly affirm divine manifestation and heart vision.
rows.anchor: الرواية كما أشرنا إليه في أخبار جنة آدم ضعيفة السند على أنها لا توافق الأصول المسلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects reading the verse as physical vision followed by a dialectical answer: it conflicts with the verse’s plain sense and Moses’ conduct, since he would have rebuked the people as ignorant as he did when they asked for an idol.
rows.anchor: فلا موجب له عليه السلام أن يلتزم كون الرؤية المذكورة في الآية سؤالا وجوابا هي الرؤية البصرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From the two reports, the author infers that Moses was not granted heart vision in earthly life but was granted it in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: أن موسى عليه السلام ما أجيب إلى الرؤية بالمعنى المذكور في الدنيا، وإنما أجيب إليها في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional about the mountain treats its endurance as parallel to Moses’ endurance: manifestation occurred to the mountain and crushed it, so Moses too would have been crushed and rendered unconscious.
rows.anchor: أن الذي فرض في الجبل هو بعينه مثل ما فرض في موسى فهو لا يطيق الظهور والإرادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine manifestation itself is possible, though for its recipient it brings collapse and unconsciousness or death; reports from the Imams abundantly describe God manifesting to the people of Paradise.
rows.anchor: فالتجلي في نفسه ممكن لكنه بالنسبة إلى المتجلي له يوجب اندكاكه وصعقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse about radiant faces looking toward their Lord is cited as evidence for the people of Paradise’s vision, alongside reports that they receive a visit every Friday.
rows.anchor: وجوه يومئذ ناضرة إلى ربها ناظرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author infers from the two reports that Moses’ ṣaʿqa was death followed by God’s return of his spirit, rather than a faint.
rows.anchor: أن صعقة موسى عليه السلام كانت موتا ثم رد الله إليه روحه لا غشية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that a tiny portion of divine light came through a needle’s eye is figurative; God’s light is neither sensory nor measurable, and the thumb-to-little-finger comparison likewise conveys its minuteness.
rows.anchor: من قبيل تمثيل المعنى بالأمور المحسوسة فلا نوره تعالى نور حسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The manifestation was only enough to crush the mountain and render Moses unconscious; God’s complete light is infinite and cannot be compared with any finite thing.
rows.anchor: وأما كمال نوره تعالى فهو غير متناه لا يحاذيه أي أمر متناه مفروض

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet illustrated the manifestation with his fingers; the mountain sank and Moses fell unconscious, with a variant saying it sinks through the earth until resurrection. Al-Tirmidhī and al-Ḥākim authenticate versions.
rows.anchor: من طرق عن أنس بن مالك أن النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم قرأ هذه الآية

rows.speaker: أئمة أهل البيت
rows.claim: Reports from the Imams say the mountain became rubble; some say it sank into the sea and continued sinking, which the author reconciles as rubble descending into the sea until no trace remained.
rows.anchor: المحصل من تفسير بعضها ببعض أنه صار رميما نزل البحر فلا يرى منه أثر أبدا

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: A report through Thābit from Anas has the Prophet indicate the measure of manifestation by touching his thumb to his little finger; when Ḥumayd challenged the narrator, he rebuked him for objecting to Anas’s report from the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وفيه أخرج أبو الشيخ وابن مردويه من طريق ثابت عن أنس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم في قوله { فلما تجلى ربه للجبل }

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports God saying that every living, dry, or wet thing that sees Him dies, collapses, or disperses, while the people of Paradise see Him without their eyes dying or bodies wearing out.
rows.anchor: لا يراني حي إلا مات، ولا يابس إلا تدهده ولا رطب إلا تفرق

rows.speaker: أبو بصير عن أبي جعفر وأبي عبد الله
rows.claim: In al-ʿAyyāshī, al-Bāqir and al-Ṣādiq report that angels warned Moses he had asked greatly; when God manifested, the mountain was crushed, Moses fell unconscious, and on regaining his spirit he declared repentance and faith.
rows.anchor: عن أبي بصير، عن أبي جعفر وأبي عبد الله عليهما السلام قال لما سأل موسى ربه تبارك وتعالى،

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Al-Ṣādiq’s report that Moses watched angelic processions of thunder, lightning, wind, and storms before asking which was his Lord is judged fabricated and incompatible with established Qurʾānic and Prophetic principles.
rows.anchor: أقول والرواية موضوعة، وما تشمل عليه لا يقبل الانطباق على شيء من مسلمات الأصول

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: A report says the Karūbiyyūn are primordial Shiʿa behind the Throne and that one of them manifested to the mountain at God’s command, making it dust.
rows.anchor: إلى أبي عبد الله عليه السلام أن الكروبيين قوم من شيعتنا من الخلق الأول جعلهم الله خلف العرش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Karūbiyyūn report means God’s manifestation can occur through intermediaries, as other divine acts occur through the Angel of Death, the trumpet blower, Michael, and Gabriel; the Karūbiyyūn are also mentioned in the Torah.
rows.anchor: أقول محصل الرواية أن تجليه سبحانه يقبل الوسائط كما أن سائر الأمور المنسوبة إليه تعالى

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Reports attribute to the Prophet two readings of “dakkan”: one with tanwīn and no lengthening, and another doubled and lengthened.
rows.anchor: عن أنس أن النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم قرء { دكا } منونة ولم يمده

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A second report attributes to the Prophet a doubled, lengthened reading of “dakka.”
rows.anchor: وفيه أخرج ابن مردويه عن أنس ان النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم قرء { فلما تجلى ربه للجبل جعله دكا } مثقلة ممدودة

rows.speaker: معاوية بن قرة عن أبيه
rows.claim: A report says six mountains flew from the force of the manifestation, three falling near Medina and three near Mecca; the author notes another transmission from Anas.
rows.anchor: عن معاوية بن قرة عن أبيه قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم فلما تجلى ربه للجبل طارت لعظمته ستة أجبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Continuing the Ibn ʿAbbās report introduced just before this segment, the author says seven mountains flew when God manifested to Moses, five in the Ḥijāz and two in Yemen.
rows.anchor: لما تجلى الله لموسى تطايرت سبعة أجبال ففي الحجاز منها خمسة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because accounts differ on the number of mountains, they do not explain the verse if they describe the mountain’s crushing; if they describe another event, isolated reports do not establish it.
rows.anchor: إن كان المراد بها تفسير دك الجبل لم ينطبق على الآية، وإن أريد غير ذلك فهو وإن كان ممكن الوقوع غير أنه لا يكفي لإثباته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Prophet says God have mercy on Moses: after hearing that his people had been tested he did not throw the tablets, but seeing them himself, he threw them and some broke; seeing is not like hearing.
rows.anchor: ليس المعاين كالمخبر أخبره ربه تبارك وتعالى أن قومه فتنوا بعده فلم يلق الألواح

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Al-Ṣādiq reports that merely hearing from God that the people had made a calf did not affect Moses as seeing them did; once he saw them, his anger intensified and he cast the tablets.
rows.anchor: لما أخبر موسى أن قومه اتخذوا عجلا

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Al-Ṣādiq adds that direct seeing has an advantage over receiving a report.
rows.anchor: قد قال أبو عبد الله عليه السلام وللرؤية فضل على الخبر

rows.speaker: علي كرم الله وجهه
rows.claim: A reading attributed to ʿAlī renders the word as “juʾār,” with an initial ḍamma and hamza, meaning a loud sound.
rows.anchor: وعن علي كرم الله وجهه أنه قرأ " جؤار " بجيم مضمومة وهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports say the tablets were made of emerald or the lote tree of Paradise, were twelve cubits long, were written while Moses heard the pens, or were preserved inside a mountain or stone in Yemen; the author regards these as unsupported isolated reports unnecessary to exegesis.
rows.anchor: وكذا ما ورد من طرق الشيعة وأهل السنة أن ألواح التوراة كانت من زبرجد

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Al-Kāfī reports from al-Bāqir that a servant who sincerely believes in God or remembers Him for forty days is made to disdain worldly life, recognize its disease and remedy, receive wisdom in the heart, and speak it.
rows.anchor: عن أبي جعفر عليه السلام قال ما أخلص عبد الإيمان بالله أربعين يوما

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: After citing the verse about the calf’s worshippers receiving divine anger and humiliation, al-Bāqir says every innovator and every fabricator against God, the Prophet, or the Ahl al-Bayt is humiliated.
rows.anchor: فلا ترى صاحب بدعة إلا ذليلا، ومفتريا على الله عز وجل وعلى رسوله وعلى أهل بيته إلا ذليلا

rows.speaker: الرضا عليه السلام
rows.claim: Al-Riḍā describes God as one without numerical implication or physical contact, manifest without being consumed by vision, and hidden without separation.
rows.anchor: أحد لا بتأويل عدد ظاهر ولا بتأويل المباشرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes that the Imams, especially ʿAlī, repeatedly speak of God’s continual manifestation to creation and refers back to his discussion under 5:73.
rows.anchor: حديث تجليه تعالى الدائم لخلقه متكرر في كلام علي والأئمة من ذريته

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Al-Ṣādiq describes God as self-subsisting, without a supporting shadow, sustaining things by their shadows, known even by the ignorant, and neither in creation nor creation in Him.
rows.anchor: لا ظل له يمسكه، وهو يمسك الأشياء بأظلتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Known to every ignorant” indicates an enduring knowledge of God in creation that does not lapse into forgetfulness or ignorance; on either reading, it is clearer that this is not inferential knowledge.
rows.anchor: ظاهر في أن له تعالى معرفة عند خلقه لا يطرأ عليها غفلة، ولا يغشاها جهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Imams’ term “shadows” means the limits that determine created things: they are not God, yet depend on His existence, and without these limits things would be void; the term may derive from the verse about shadows.
rows.anchor: الأظلة والظلال اصطلاح منهم عليهم السلام والمراد بظل الشيء حده

rows.speaker: علي عليه السلام
rows.claim: ʿAlī says God is too great to be veiled from anything or to have anything veiled from Him, and that he sees God before every thing he sees.
rows.anchor: إن الله أجل من أن يحتجب عن شيء أو يحتجب عنه شيء

rows.speaker: علي عليه السلام
rows.claim: ʿAlī says he never worshipped a Lord he had not seen; the Nahj explains that eyes do not see God through ocular vision, while hearts see Him through the realities of faith.
rows.anchor: ولكن رأته القلوب بحقائق الإيمان

rows.speaker: أبو بصير عن أبي عبد الله
rows.claim: Asked whether believers see God on Judgment Day, al-Ṣādiq answers that they saw Him earlier, at the primordial covenant when they affirmed “Am I not your Lord?”, and that believers see Him in worldly life too.
rows.anchor: حين قال لهم { ألست بربكم؟ قالوا بلى } ثم سكت ساعة ثم قال وإن المؤمنين ليرونه في الدنيا

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: In the continuation of the report, al-Ṣādiq confirms that the questioner can see God at that moment, but warns against publicizing this lest an ignorant listener mistake heart vision for likeness or bodily vision.
rows.anchor: ألست تراه في وقتك هذا؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Heart vision is neither acquired belief by inference nor sensory sight; it is direct apprehension through conscious witnessing, though ordinary usage is avoided because people hear “vision” as physical sight.
rows.anchor: فحقيقة الرؤية ثابتة وهي نيل الشيء بالمشاهدة العلمية من غير طريق الاستدلال الفكري

rows.speaker: موسى بن جعفر
rows.claim: Al-Kāẓim says creation is the only veil between God and His creatures: God is veiled without an actual concealing barrier and hidden without a covering.
rows.anchor: ليس بينه وبين خلقه حجاب غير خلقه فقد احتجب بغير حجاب محجوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report means God is continuously witnessed and known, but people’s attention to themselves hides their awareness of that witnessing: knowledge is always present, while awareness of knowing can lapse.
rows.anchor: العلم بالعلم مفقود في بعض الأحيان

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: When al-Ṣādiq asked a doubter whether, alone on a broken ship’s plank amid waves and cut off from every rescue, his heart clung to anything, the man said yes; al-Ṣādiq identified that object as God.
rows.anchor: هل تعلق قلبك إذ ذاك بشيء

rows.speaker: الرضا عليه السلام
rows.claim: Al-Riḍā says God’s creation of creatures forms a veil between Him and them.
rows.anchor: خلقة الله الخلق حجاب بينه وبينهم

rows.speaker: علي بن الحسين
rows.claim: Asked why God veiled creatures from Himself, al-Sajjād answers that God created them upon ignorance; the author explains this as creating them so they become occupied with themselves.
rows.anchor: لأن الله تبارك وتعالى بناهم بنية على الجهل

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Al-Bāqir says God existed when nothing else did as light without darkness, truthful without falsehood, knowing without ignorance, and living without death, and remains so forever.
rows.anchor: كان ولا شيء غيره نورا لا ظلام فيه

rows.speaker: الرضا عليه السلام
rows.claim: Al-Riḍā says that when the Prophet looked at his Lord with his heart, God placed him in a light like the light of the veils, enabling him to perceive what was within them.
rows.anchor: إذا نظر إلى ربه بقلبه جعله في نور مثل نور الحجب حتى يستبين له ما في الحجب

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Asked whether the Prophet saw his Lord, al-Kāẓim answers that he saw Him with his heart, citing 53:11: he did not see Him by eyesight but by the heart.
rows.anchor: لم يره بالبصر ولكن رآه بالفؤاد

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الأعلى مولى آل سام
rows.claim: A report from al-Ṣādiq calls it polytheism to claim God is known through a veil, image, or likeness; God is known only through God, and every creature apprehends things through Him.
rows.anchor: ومن زعم أنه يعرف الله بحجاب أو بصورة أو بمثال فهو مشرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report rejects inferential knowledge as the only knowledge of God: every creature that apprehends anything already knows God, while restricting knowledge to proofs risks ignorance and hidden associationism.
rows.anchor: تثبت معرفة الله لكل مخلوق يدرك شيئا ما من الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowing an object through a supposed intermediary actually apprehends the intermediary; treating this as knowledge of the object would require the intermediary to be both identical with and distinct from it, making knowledge ineffective.
rows.anchor: فالذي تعلق به إدراكنا هو الوسط دون الظرف الذي هو ذو وسط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since no intermediary links Creator and creature, God can only be known through Himself; because God is in fact known, His essence and being known are one, so He cannot be unknown.
rows.anchor: فالله سبحانه لو عرف عرف بذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A created thing cannot exist independently from God in reality or thought; every knower and known object depends on Him, so the knower encounters God before the object and knows it through God.
rows.anchor: لا يستقل عنه تعالى بذاته بوجه من الوجوه لا في خارج ولا في ذهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is needed for the knower to know and for the object to be known: God is first the known and knower, with other things known or knowing through Him secondarily.
rows.anchor: أي أن الله سبحانه هو المعلوم أولا ويعلم به المعلوم ثانيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report’s “veil” is a supposed separator, “image” a sensory-featured mental image, and “likeness” a non-sensory rational concept; alternatively these terms mean sensory or imagined images, or conception and assent. All such discursive knowledge is excluded.
rows.anchor: وبالصورة الصورة الذهنية المقارنة للأوصاف المحسوسة من الأضواء والألوان والأقدار وبالمثال ما هو من المعاني العقلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling conceptual knowledge of God associationism follows because it inserts a mediator that is neither Creator nor creature, making it a partner; sharing a meaning while differing in existence also makes the known composite and compromises divine unity.
rows.anchor: أي أنه لا يشاركه في ذاته شيء بوجه من الوجوه
